claim: FSHD type 1 (FSHD1) is caused by having fewer than 11 D4Z4 repeats combined with a permissive chromosome 4qA haplotype.

source: Pharmacological inhibition of HDAC1/HDAC2 activity by MS-275 (Nebbioso et al., 2009) also increased DUX4 and DUX4 target gene expression, and enhanced histone H4 acetylation at the D4Z4 array (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Pharmacological inhibition of HDAC1/HDAC2 activity by MS-275 enhanced histone H4 acetylation at the D4Z4 array.
source: Pharmacological inhibition of HDAC1/HDAC2 activity by MS-275 (Nebbioso et al., 2009) also increased DUX4 and DUX4 target gene expression, and enhanced histone H4 acetylation at the D4Z4 array (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B.

claim: HDAC1 and HDAC2 are associated with and function to transcriptionally repress the D4Z4 array.
source: Collectively, these results indicate that HDAC1 and HDAC2 are associated with, and function to transcriptionally repress, the D4Z4 array.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the knockdown and pharmacological inhibition experiments.

claim: The D4Z4 repeat in control myoblasts is more resistant to de-repression than the D4Z4 repeat in FSHD cells.
source: These data also show that the D4Z4 repeat in control myoblasts is more resistant to de-repression than the D4Z4 repeat in FSHD cells, which are sensitized because of a shortened array (FSHD1) or SMCHD1 mutation (FSHD2).
evidence: This is inferred from the differential response to HDAC knockdown in control versus FSHD cells.

claim: CHD4 knockdown in MB073 FSHD1 myoblasts increased DUX4 mRNA 20-fold.
source: However, CHD4 knockdown in MB073 FSHD1 or MB200 FSHD2 myoblasts increased DUX4 mRNA 20-fold and concomitantly activated DUX4 targets (Figure 2F–G and Figure 2—figure supplement 3B–C).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: CHD4 knockdown in MB200 FSHD2 myoblasts increased DUX4 mRNA 20-fold.
source: However, CHD4 knockdown in MB073 FSHD1 or MB200 FSHD2 myoblasts increased DUX4 mRNA 20-fold and concomitantly activated DUX4 targets (Figure 2F–G and Figure 2—figure supplement 3B–C).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: CHD3 depletion did not lead to DUX4 de-repression in either control or FSHD cells.
source: In contrast, CHD3 depletion did not lead to DUX4 de-repression in either control or FSHD cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 4), consistent with its absence from the gD4Z4 enChIP purifications and the mutually exclusive nature of CHD3 and CHD4 within the NuRD complex.
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: CHD4 binds the D4Z4 repeat and is necessary to silence DUX4 expression in FSHD cells.
source: Together, these results reveal that CHD4 binds the D4Z4 repeat and is necessary to silence DUX4 expression in FSHD cells, whereas control myoblasts have a more stably repressed D4Z4 array.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the enChIP-MS, ChIP, and knockdown data.

claim: Depleting MBD2 from MB073 FSHD1 myoblasts moderately but significantly increased DUX4 expression.
source: However, depleting MBD2 from MB073 FSHD1 myoblasts moderately, but significantly, increased DUX4 expression, whereas DUX4 was not de-repressed when MBD2 was knocked down in MB200 FSHD2 myoblasts (Figure 2I–J and Figure 2—figure supplement 5B–C).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2I.

claim: DUX4 was not de-repressed when MBD2 was knocked down in MB200 FSHD2 myoblasts.
source: However, depleting MBD2 from MB073 FSHD1 myoblasts moderately, but significantly, increased DUX4 expression, whereas DUX4 was not de-repressed when MBD2 was knocked down in MB200 FSHD2 myoblasts (Figure 2I–J and Figure 2—figure supplement 5B–C).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2J.

claim: Depletion of MBD3 did not de-repress DUX4 in MB2401 control, MB073 FSHD1 or MB200 FSHD2 myoblasts.
source: We further observed that depletion of MBD3, which can recruit the NuRD complex to unmethylated DNA (Baubec et al., 2013; Le Guezennec et al., 2006; Saito and Ishikawa, 2002), did not de-repress DUX4 in MB2401 control, MB073 FSHD1 or MB200 FSHD2 myoblasts (Figure 2—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 6.

claim: MBD2 occupies the D4Z4 array and is necessary for DUX4 repression in at least some contexts.
source: Together, these data show that MBD2 occupies the D4Z4 array and is necessary for DUX4 repression in at least some contexts, and suggest that factors in addition to MBD2 might recruit components shared by the NuRD complex to silence the D4Z4 macrosatellite repeat.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the ChIP and knockdown data showing context-dependent effects.

claim: The NuRD complex and the CAF-1 chromatin assembly complex work together in several molecular processes.
source: The NuRD complex is known to cooperate with other complexes to carry out its cellular functions. For example, NuRD and the CAF-1 chromatin assembly complex work together in several molecular processes (Helbling Chadwick et al., 2009; Yang et al., 2015) and share a core subunit, RBBP4, which was identified as associated with the D4Z4 repeat by gD4Z4 enChIP purification (Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: NuRD and CAF-1 share a core subunit, RBBP4.
source: The NuRD complex is known to cooperate with other complexes to carry out its cellular functions. For example, NuRD and the CAF-1 chromatin assembly complex work together in several molecular processes (Helbling Chadwick et al., 2009; Yang et al., 2015) and share a core subunit, RBBP4, which was identified as associated with the D4Z4 repeat by gD4Z4 enChIP purification (Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by citations and confirmed by enChIP-MS data.

claim: RBBP4 was identified as associated with the D4Z4 repeat by gD4Z4 enChIP purification.
source: The NuRD complex is known to cooperate with other complexes to carry out its cellular functions. For example, NuRD and the CAF-1 chromatin assembly complex work together in several molecular processes (Helbling Chadwick et al., 2009; Yang et al., 2015) and share a core subunit, RBBP4, which was identified as associated with the D4Z4 repeat by gD4Z4 enChIP purification (Table 1).
evidence: This is a direct result from the mass spectrometry data.

claim: Depleting CHAF1A or CHAF1B resulted in the activation of DUX4 and DUX4 target genes in FSHD myoblasts.
source: Depleting CHAF1A or CHAF1B resulted in the activation of DUX4 and DUX4 target genes in FSHD myoblasts (Figure 3B–D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1), confirming a role for this complex in D4Z4 regulation.
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figures 3B-D.

claim: CAF-1 interacts with CpG-binding protein MBD1, which binds both methylated and unmethylated DNA to inhibit transcription.
source: CAF-1 interacts with CpG-binding protein MBD1, which binds both methylated and unmethylated DNA to inhibit transcription (Jørgensen et al., 2004; Reese et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Knockdown of MBD1 led to DUX4 and DUX4 target gene activation in MB200 FSHD2 myoblasts but not in MB2401 control or MB073 FSHD1 myoblasts.
source: Knockdown of MBD1 led to DUX4 and DUX4 target gene activation in MB200 FSHD2 myoblasts but not in MB2401 control or MB073 FSHD1 myoblasts (Figure 3E–G and Figure 3—figure supplement 2), indicating a possible context-dependent relative necessity of MBD1 or MBD2 in different FSHD cells.
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figures 3E-G.

claim: Simultaneous depletion of CHAF1A and CHD4 increased DUX4 mRNA levels over 150-fold in MB2401 control myoblasts.
source: Notably, although knockdown of CHAF1A or CHD4 alone did not induce DUX4 expression in MB2401 control myoblasts (Figure 2E and Figure 3B), simultaneous depletion increased DUX4 mRNA levels over 150-fold (Figure 3H and Figure 3—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: Dual CHD4 and CHAF1A knockdown had an additive or greater impact in MB073 FSHD1 and MB200 FSHD2 myoblasts compared to singular knockdown.
source: An additive or greater impact was also observed with dual versus singular CHD4 and CHAF1A knockdown in MB073 FSHD1 and MB200 FSHD2 myoblasts (Figure 3I–J and Figure 3—figure supplement 3B–C).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figures 3I-J.

claim: A combination of MBD1- and MBD2-mediated recruitment of the CAF-1 and NuRD repressive complexes work together to silence the D4Z4 repeat in skeletal muscle cells.
source: Together, these results indicate that a combination of MBD1- and MBD2-mediated recruitment of the CAF-1 and NuRD repressive complexes, respectively, work together to silence the D4Z4 repeat in skeletal muscle cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the knockdown experiments showing context-dependent roles of MBD1 and MBD2.

claim: All five additional FSHD cell lines tested showed de-repression of DUX4 upon knockdown of MBD2 or CHAF1A.
source: All five lines showed de-repression of DUX4 upon knockdown of MBD2 or CHAF1A, and all but one (2453, an FSHD2 cell line) showed increased DUX4 expression following CHD4 depletion, whereas de-repression following MBD1 knockdown was evident in the FSHD1 and two of the FSHD2 cell lines (Figure 3—figure supplements 4–7).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 3—figure supplements 4-7.

claim: All but one FSHD cell line (2453) showed increased DUX4 expression following CHD4 depletion.
source: All five lines showed de-repression of DUX4 upon knockdown of MBD2 or CHAF1A, and all but one (2453, an FSHD2 cell line) showed increased DUX4 expression following CHD4 depletion, whereas de-repression following MBD1 knockdown was evident in the FSHD1 and two of the FSHD2 cell lines (Figure 3—figure supplements 4–7).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 3—figure supplements 4-7.

claim: De-repression following MBD1 knockdown was evident in the FSHD1 and two of the FSHD2 cell lines.
source: All five lines showed de-repression of DUX4 upon knockdown of MBD2 or CHAF1A, and all but one (2453, an FSHD2 cell line) showed increased DUX4 expression following CHD4 depletion, whereas de-repression following MBD1 knockdown was evident in the FSHD1 and two of the FSHD2 cell lines (Figure 3—figure supplements 4–7).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 3—figure supplements 4-7.

claim: The NuRD and CAF-1 complexes have combined roles in repressing DUX4.
source: Taken together, these data indicate the combined roles of the NuRD and CAF-1 complexes in repressing DUX4, and that the relative necessity of specific components of each pathway might vary depending on the cellular context, or possibly the efficiency of each knockdown.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the knockdown experiments across multiple cell lines.

claim: TRIM28, SETDB1, and KDM1A are shared auxiliary factors utilized by core members of the NuRD and CAF-1 complexes to repress transcription.
source: To repress transcription, core members of the NuRD and CAF-1 complexes utilize a shared set of auxiliary factors, namely the tripartite motif-containing protein TRIM28, the lysine methyltransferase SETDB1, and the lysine demethylase KDM1A (Ivanov et al., 2007; Loyola et al., 2009; Sarraf and Stancheva, 2004; Schultz et al., 2001; Wang et al., 2009; Yang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Knockdown of TRIM28, SETDB1 or KDM1A de-repressed DUX4 in MB073 FSHD1 and MB200 FSHD2 myoblasts to varying degrees ranging from 3- to 130-fold.
source: Knockdown of TRIM28, SETDB1 or KDM1A de-repressed DUX4 in MB073 FSHD1 and MB200 FSHD2 myoblasts to varying degrees ranging from 3- to 130-fold (Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplements 1–3), implicating them in facilitating silencing of the D4Z4 array.
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Only KDM1A knockdown de-repressed DUX4 mRNA in MB2401 control myoblasts.
source: Of these factors, only KDM1A knockdown de-repressed DUX4 mRNA in the MB2401 control myoblasts, indicating a necessary role for this demethylase in maintaining repression of both normal and pathological D4Z4 alleles in muscle cells.
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: KDM1A has a necessary role in maintaining repression of both normal and pathological D4Z4 alleles in muscle cells.
source: Of these factors, only KDM1A knockdown de-repressed DUX4 mRNA in the MB2401 control myoblasts, indicating a necessary role for this demethylase in maintaining repression of both normal and pathological D4Z4 alleles in muscle cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the knockdown data showing KDM1A is required in both control and FSHD cells.

claim: Depletion of SIN3A or SIN3B led to the activation of DUX4 and DUX4 target genes in FSHD cells.
source: Therefore, we tested its role in D4Z4 repeat repression and found that SIN3A or SIN3B depletion led to the activation of DUX4 and DUX4 target genes in FSHD cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 4B–G), supporting a role for the SIN3 complex in D4Z4 regulation.
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claim: D4Z4 array silencing is mediated by multiple chromatin regulatory factors that act together with core components of the NuRD complex and depend on the CAF-1 chromatin assembly complex.
source: Taken together, these data indicate that D4Z4 array silencing is mediated by multiple chromatin regulatory factors that act together with core components of the NuRD complex and also depend on the CAF-1 chromatin assembly complex to achieve full epigenetic repression.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the knockdown experiments showing multiple factors are required.

claim: DUX4 is expressed at very low levels in human iPS cell populations.
source: We previously reported that DUX4 is expressed at very low levels in human iPS cell populations (Snider et al., 2010) and, similar to the expression pattern in FSHD myoblasts, this represents the occasional expression in a small number of cells (JWL, unpublished data).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work and unpublished data.

claim: DUX4 is present in four-cell human embryos.
source: We have more recently shown that DUX4 is present in four-cell human embryos and that when expressed in iPS cells or muscle cells it activates a cleavage-stage transcriptional program similar to the program expressed in a subset of 'naïve' iPS or embryonic stem (ES) cells (Hendrickson et al., 2017; Whiddon et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: When expressed in iPS cells or muscle cells, DUX4 activates a cleavage-stage transcriptional program similar to the program expressed in a subset of 'naïve' iPS or embryonic stem (ES) cells.
source: We have more recently shown that DUX4 is present in four-cell human embryos and that when expressed in iPS cells or muscle cells it activates a cleavage-stage transcriptional program similar to the program expressed in a subset of 'naïve' iPS or embryonic stem (ES) cells (Hendrickson et al., 2017; Whiddon et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Depletion of HDAC1/HDAC2, CHD4, CHAF1A, SETDB1 or SIN3B de-repressed DUX4 in human eMHF2 iPS cells.
source: Similar to our myoblast results, depletion of HDAC1/HDAC2, CHD4, CHAF1A, SETDB1 or SIN3B de-repressed DUX4 in iPS cells; whereas, unlike in myoblasts, knockdown of KDM1A in iPS cells had a more minor effect on the levels of DUX4 mRNA (Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Knockdown of KDM1A in iPS cells had a more minor effect on the levels of DUX4 mRNA compared to myoblasts.
source: Similar to our myoblast results, depletion of HDAC1/HDAC2, CHD4, CHAF1A, SETDB1 or SIN3B de-repressed DUX4 in iPS cells; whereas, unlike in myoblasts, knockdown of KDM1A in iPS cells had a more minor effect on the levels of DUX4 mRNA (Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Depletion of NuRD and CAF-1 complex components did not lead to DUX4 de-repression in the parental HFF3 fibroblast line.
source: Notably, depletion of NuRD and CAF-1 complex components did not lead to DUX4 de-repression in the parental HFF3 fibroblast line, whereas the HFF3 iPS lines responded similarly to the eMHF2 iPS line (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: HFF3 iPS lines responded similarly to the eMHF2 iPS line upon depletion of NuRD and CAF-1 complex components.
source: Notably, depletion of NuRD and CAF-1 complex components did not lead to DUX4 de-repression in the parental HFF3 fibroblast line, whereas the HFF3 iPS lines responded similarly to the eMHF2 iPS line (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: The NuRD and CAF-1 complexes that silence the D4Z4 macrosatellite array in muscle cells also contribute to the regulation of this locus in human iPS cells.
source: These results indicate that the NuRD and CAF-1 complexes that silence the D4Z4 macrosatellite array in muscle cells also contribute to the regulation of this locus in human iPS cells, and that iPS cells have decreased D4Z4 repression compared to their somatic counterpart, similar to the decreased repression in FSHD myoblasts compared to control myoblasts.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the knockdown experiments in iPS cells.

claim: iPS cells have decreased D4Z4 repression compared to their somatic counterpart.
source: These results indicate that the NuRD and CAF-1 complexes that silence the D4Z4 macrosatellite array in muscle cells also contribute to the regulation of this locus in human iPS cells, and that iPS cells have decreased D4Z4 repression compared to their somatic counterpart, similar to the decreased repression in FSHD myoblasts compared to control myoblasts.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential response to knockdown in fibroblasts versus iPS cells.

claim: The MBD3L family (MBD3L2, MBD3L3, MBD3L4, and MBD3L5) is a direct target of DUX4.
source: In prior studies of DUX4-induced gene expression, we identified the MBD3L family (MBD3L2, MBD3L3, MBD3L4, and MBD3L5) as a direct target of DUX4 that was expressed in FSHD, but not control, muscle cells and muscle biopsies, and activated by exogenous DUX4 in cultured human myoblasts (Geng et al., 2012; Yao et al., 2014; Young et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The MBD3L family was expressed in FSHD, but not control, muscle cells and muscle biopsies.
source: In prior studies of DUX4-induced gene expression, we identified the MBD3L family (MBD3L2, MBD3L3, MBD3L4, and MBD3L5) as a direct target of DUX4 that was expressed in FSHD, but not control, muscle cells and muscle biopsies, and activated by exogenous DUX4 in cultured human myoblasts (Geng et al., 2012; Yao et al., 2014; Young et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: MBD3L family proteins can replace MBD2 or MBD3 in the NuRD complex but they lack the CpG-binding domain.
source: MBD3L family proteins can replace MBD2 or MBD3 in the NuRD complex but they lack the CpG-binding domain and antagonize NuRD-mediated transcriptional repression, possibly by preventing the complex from being recruited to its DNA targets (Jiang et al., 2002; Jin et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: MBD3L family proteins antagonize NuRD-mediated transcriptional repression, possibly by preventing the complex from being recruited to its DNA targets.
source: MBD3L family proteins can replace MBD2 or MBD3 in the NuRD complex but they lack the CpG-binding domain and antagonize NuRD-mediated transcriptional repression, possibly by preventing the complex from being recruited to its DNA targets (Jiang et al., 2002; Jin et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Expression of MBD3L2 induced DUX4 5–18-fold in MB073 FSHD1 and MB200 FSHD2 myoblasts.
source: Similar to the knockdown of NuRD complex members, expression of MBD3L2 induced DUX4 5–18-fold in MB073 FSHD1 and MB200 FSHD2 myoblasts and increased by 10-fold the number of myoblast nuclei expressing DUX4 protein, whereas DUX4 was not de-repressed in MB2401 control myoblasts (Figure 6A–E and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figures 6B-C.

claim: Expression of MBD3L2 increased by 10-fold the number of myoblast nuclei expressing DUX4 protein in FSHD myoblasts.
source: Similar to the knockdown of NuRD complex members, expression of MBD3L2 induced DUX4 5–18-fold in MB073 FSHD1 and MB200 FSHD2 myoblasts and increased by 10-fold the number of myoblast nuclei expressing DUX4 protein, whereas DUX4 was not de-repressed in MB2401 control myoblasts (Figure 6A–E and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figures 6D-E.

claim: DUX4 was not de-repressed by MBD3L2 expression in MB2401 control myoblasts.
source: Similar to the knockdown of NuRD complex members, expression of MBD3L2 induced DUX4 5–18-fold in MB073 FSHD1 and MB200 FSHD2 myoblasts and increased by 10-fold the number of myoblast nuclei expressing DUX4 protein, whereas DUX4 was not de-repressed in MB2401 control myoblasts (Figure 6A–E and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: DUX4 expression increases in FSHD myotubes compared to myoblasts.
source: When cultured in low mitogen differentiation media, myoblasts fuse to form multinucleated myotubes, and DUX4 expression increases in FSHD myotubes compared to myoblasts (Balog et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: shRNA inhibition of MBD3L RNAs in MB073 FSHD1 and MB200 FSHD2 myotubes decreased DUX4 and DUX4 target gene expression by ~50% and ~30%, respectively.
source: To determine whether the DUX4-induced MBD3L proteins might contribute to the increased DUX4 expression in myotubes, we expressed short hairpin RNA (shRNA) to inhibit MBD3L RNAs in MB073 FSHD1 and MB200 FSHD2 myotubes and found that these decreased DUX4 and DUX4 target gene expression by ~50% and~30%, respectively (Figure 6F–G, Figure 6—figure supplement 1D–E and Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figures 6F-G.

claim: Endogenous DUX4-induced MBD3L proteins contribute to the amplification of DUX4 expression in FSHD myotubes.
source: Together, these data implicate MBD3L2 in the regulation of the D4Z4 array and demonstrate that endogenous DUX4-induced MBD3L proteins contribute to the amplification of DUX4 expression in FSHD myotubes.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the overexpression and knockdown experiments.

claim: Each complex (NuRD and CAF-1) appears to have a parallel, or redundant, function in DUX4 repression because knockdown of both pathways was necessary to induce DUX4 expression in MB2401 control myoblasts.
source: To some extent, each complex appears to have a parallel, or redundant, function in DUX4 repression because knockdown of both pathways was necessary to induce DUX4 expression in MB2401 control myoblasts.
evidence: This is inferred from the dual knockdown experiments showing additive effects.

claim: The distinctive mutations causing FSHD might preferentially weaken different specific components of the NuRD or CAF-1 pathways.
source: The distinctive mutations causing FSHD, or other factors such as the distribution of DNA methylation on the D4Z4, might preferentially weaken different specific components of each pathway, as evidenced by the relative necessity for CHD4, MBD2 or MBD1 in different FSHD cell lines.
evidence: This is speculated based on the variable responses to knockdown in different FSHD cell lines.

claim: The NuRD and CAF-1 complexes together are necessary to maintain D4Z4 repression.
source: Overall, despite the relative differences in the necessity of the specific protein knockdown of individual components of the NuRD or CAF-1 complexes in different FSHD cells, the data show that these complexes together are necessary to maintain D4Z4 repression.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the knockdown experiments across multiple cell lines.

claim: The enChIP pulldowns identified several D4Z4-associated proteins that are involved in epigenetic silencing of variegated gene expression in mice.
source: Our en-ChIP pulldowns identified several D4Z4-associated proteins that are involved in epigenetic silencing of variegated gene expression in mice (Blewitt et al., 2005; Daxinger et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work on Momme genes.

claim: Smchd1 was shown to directly repress DUX4 in human cells and to be a causative gene for FSHD2.
source: One of this group of Modifier of murine metastable epiallele (Momme) genes, Smchd1, was shown to directly repress DUX4 in human cells and to be a causative gene for FSHD2 (Lemmers et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The Momme genes PBRM1, RIF1, SMARCA4, SMARCA5 and UHRF1 were identified as D4Z4-associated by enChIP-MS.
source: In addition to finding SMCHD1 associated with the D4Z4 in our enChIP, we identified the Momme genes PBRM1, RIF1, SMARCA4, SMARCA5 and UHRF1 as D4Z4-associated by enChIP-MS, and implicated the Momme genes HDAC1, SETDB1 and TRIM28 in the regulation of DUX4 through knockdown experiments.
evidence: This is a direct result from the mass spectrometry data.

claim: The Momme genes HDAC1, SETDB1 and TRIM28 were implicated in the regulation of DUX4 through knockdown experiments.
source: In addition to finding SMCHD1 associated with the D4Z4 in our enChIP, we identified the Momme genes PBRM1, RIF1, SMARCA4, SMARCA5 and UHRF1 as D4Z4-associated by enChIP-MS, and implicated the Momme genes HDAC1, SETDB1 and TRIM28 in the regulation of DUX4 through knockdown experiments.
evidence: This is supported by the knockdown experiments showing DUX4 de-repression.

claim: Conserved machinery may be responsible for repressing variegated gene expression across species.
source: The convergence and striking overlap of the results of these two complementary approaches to understanding variegated gene expression suggest that conserved machinery may be responsible for repressing this type of locus across species.
evidence: This is speculated based on the overlap between Momme genes and D4Z4-associated proteins.

claim: The presence of chromatin remodelers and positive transcriptional regulators at the D4Z4 locus indicates a dynamic balance between activators and repressors.
source: The presence of chromatin remodelers and positive transcriptional regulators, such as SMARCA5, BRD3 and BRD4, at the D4Z4 locus in the control cells used for the enChIP also indicates a dynamic balance between activators and repressors, which is consistent with the identification of sense and anti-sense transcripts associated with the D4Z4 repeats in both control and FSHD cells (Snider et al., 2010).
evidence: This is inferred from the enChIP-MS data and supported by a citation.

claim: The necessity of the NuRD complex to maintain repression of DUX4 in FSHD cells suggests that the DUX4-mediated induction of the MBD3L family of factors might amplify DUX4 expression within a nucleus or facilitate the internuclear spreading of DUX4 in multinucleated myotubes.
source: The necessity of the NuRD complex to maintain repression of DUX4 in FSHD cells suggests that the DUX4-mediated induction of the MBD3L family of factors might amplify DUX4 expression within a nucleus or facilitate the internuclear spreading of DUX4 in multinucleated myotubes.
evidence: This is speculated based on the knockdown and overexpression data.

claim: MBD3L factors replace MBD2 or MBD3 in the NuRD complex and antagonize its normal repressive function.
source: MBD3L factors replace MBD2 or MBD3 in the NuRD complex and antagonize its normal repressive function (Jiang et al., 2002; Jin et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Expression of MBD3L2 was sufficient to amplify DUX4 expression in FSHD cells.
source: In this study, we showed that expression of MBD3L2 was sufficient to amplify DUX4 expression in FSHD cells and knockdown using an shRNA that targets the entire family showed that expression of the MBD3L family was necessary for the full induction of DUX4 expression in FSHD myotubes.
evidence: This is supported by the overexpression experiments.

claim: Expression of the MBD3L family was necessary for the full induction of DUX4 expression in FSHD myotubes.
source: In this study, we showed that expression of MBD3L2 was sufficient to amplify DUX4 expression in FSHD cells and knockdown using an shRNA that targets the entire family showed that expression of the MBD3L family was necessary for the full induction of DUX4 expression in FSHD myotubes.
evidence: This is supported by the shRNA knockdown experiments.

claim: DUX4 induces high expression of the clustered MBD3L genes, revealing a positive feed-forward mechanism.
source: The fact that DUX4 induces high expression of the clustered MBD3L genes reveals a positive feed-forward mechanism that might facilitate spreading of DUX4 expression between nuclei in myotubes.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing DUX4 induces MBD3L and MBD3L amplifies DUX4.

claim: In FSHD myotubes, DUX4 expression apparently initiates in a single nucleus and the protein then spreads to adjacent nuclei in the syncytium.
source: In FSHD myotubes, DUX4 expression apparently initiates in a single nucleus and the protein then spreads to adjacent nuclei in the syncytium.
evidence: This is stated as an observation, likely based on prior unpublished data or general knowledge.

claim: MBD3L proteins are detected as spreading to adjacent nuclei in myotubes.
source: Similarly, MBD3L proteins are detected as spreading to adjacent nuclei (AEC, unpublished data) where they would facilitate DUX4 expression.
evidence: This is based on unpublished data.

claim: Each DUX4 expressing nucleus would act to progressively amplify DUX4 expression in its neighbors, spreading DUX4 expression along the myofiber.
source: In this manner, each DUX4 expressing nucleus would act to progressively amplify DUX4 expression in its neighbors, spreading DUX4 expression along the myofiber.
evidence: This is a mechanistic model inferred from the data.

claim: The DUX4-mediated inhibition of NMD can amplify DUX4 expression by stabilizing the DUX4 mRNA, which is itself a target of NMD.
source: This might be similar to, and additive with, the prior observation that the DUX4-mediated inhibition of NMD can amplify DUX4 expression by stabilizing the DUX4 mRNA, which is itself a target of NMD (Feng et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The internuclear amplification of DUX4 expression might contribute to the susceptibility of skeletal muscle to damage in FSHD.
source: It is interesting to speculate that the internuclear amplification of DUX4 expression might contribute to the susceptibility of skeletal muscle to damage in FSHD.
evidence: This is explicitly stated as speculation.

claim: One therapeutic strategy would be to enhance D4Z4 repression by designing drugs that increase NuRD complex-mediated repression.
source: One strategy would be to enhance D4Z4 repression by designing drugs that increase NuRD complex-mediated repression.
evidence: This is a proposed therapeutic strategy based on the findings.

claim: Mutations in SMCHD1 and DNMT3B that cause FSHD have limited genome-wide consequences, suggesting that some factors might be relatively specific for repressing repetitive regions of the genome.
source: This is partly due to concerns that they might also suppress important tumor suppressor genes, but the fact that mutations in SMCHD1 and DNMT3B that cause FSHD have limited genome-wide consequences suggests that some factors might be relatively specific for repressing repetitive regions of the genome.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that FSHD-causing mutations have limited effects.

claim: A second therapeutic strategy would be to prevent the amplification of DUX4 after it stochastically 'bursts' on in a myotube nucleus by inhibiting the production of MBD3L proteins with small molecules or interfering RNAs.
source: A second strategy would be to prevent the amplification of DUX4 after it stochastically 'bursts' on in a myotube nucleus. This might be accomplished by inhibiting the production of MBD3L proteins with small molecules or interfering RNAs.
evidence: This is a proposed therapeutic strategy based on the findings.

claim: Myoblast transplantation with cells containing larger D4Z4 repeat sizes or 4qB alleles might provide 'decoy' nuclei that would absorb MBD3L factors and not activate DUX4.
source: Alternatively, myoblast transplantation with cells containing larger D4Z4 repeat sizes or 4qB alleles might provide 'decoy' nuclei that would absorb MBD3L factors and not activate DUX4, or, in a similar decoy approach, autologous transplants following deletion of the D4Z4 array and/or the MBD3L cluster.
evidence: This is a proposed therapeutic strategy based on the findings.

claim: The expression of DUX4 in a small percentage of iPS cells or ES cells shares mechanisms of molecular regulation with skeletal muscle cells.
source: Although little is known about the regulation of DUX4 expression in cleavage-stage embryos and the testis luminal cells, it is evident from this study that the expression of DUX4 in a small percentage of iPS cells or ES cells shares mechanisms of molecular regulation with skeletal muscle cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the knockdown experiments in iPS cells.

claim: There are similarities between the regulation of the human DUX4 retrogene and the mouse Dux retrogene.
source: This also indicates similarities between the regulation of the human DUX4 retrogene and the mouse Dux retrogene that is also in a macrosatellite array, although thought to have arisen from a separate retrotransposition of the DUXC gene (Clapp et al., 2007; Leidenroth et al., 2012; Leidenroth and Hewitt, 2010).
evidence: This is inferred from the similarities in regulation and supported by citations.

claim: CAF-1 depletion in mouse ES cells resulted in the expression of genes specific to two-cell embryos.
source: It was previously shown that CAF-1 depletion in mouse ES cells resulted in the expression of genes specific to two-cell embryos (Ishiuchi et al., 2015), and later shown that induction of these genes was blocked by simultaneous knockdown of mouse Dux along with Chaf1a (Hendrickson et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Induction of two-cell embryo genes in mouse ES cells was blocked by simultaneous knockdown of mouse Dux along with Chaf1a.
source: It was previously shown that CAF-1 depletion in mouse ES cells resulted in the expression of genes specific to two-cell embryos (Ishiuchi et al., 2015), and later shown that induction of these genes was blocked by simultaneous knockdown of mouse Dux along with Chaf1a (Hendrickson et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Trim28, Kdm1a, and HDAC inhibitors have been shown to regulate Zscan4 and the early cleavage program in mouse ES cells.
source: Trim28, Kdm1a, and HDAC inhibitors have been shown to regulate Zscan4 and the early cleavage program in mouse ES cells (Macfarlan et al., 2012), and for Trim28 this activity was shown to be mediated through the induction of mouse Dux (De Iaco et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: For Trim28, regulation of Zscan4 and the early cleavage program was shown to be mediated through the induction of mouse Dux.
source: Trim28, Kdm1a, and HDAC inhibitors have been shown to regulate Zscan4 and the early cleavage program in mouse ES cells (Macfarlan et al., 2012), and for Trim28 this activity was shown to be mediated through the induction of mouse Dux (De Iaco et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The NuRD complex and MBD3 have been shown to inhibit cellular reprogramming in mouse ES cells.
source: Similarly, the NuRD complex and MBD3 have been shown to inhibit cellular reprogramming in mouse ES cells, and, conversely, reprogramming to a naive stem cell state was facilitated by inhibition of these complexes (Luo et al., 2013; Rais et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Reprogramming to a naive stem cell state was facilitated by inhibition of the NuRD complex.
source: Similarly, the NuRD complex and MBD3 have been shown to inhibit cellular reprogramming in mouse ES cells, and, conversely, reprogramming to a naive stem cell state was facilitated by inhibition of these complexes (Luo et al., 2013; Rais et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Inhibiting NuRD or CAF-1 activity potentiates stem cell reprogramming in mouse ES/iPS cells.
source: The fact that inhibiting NuRD or CAF-1 activity potentiates stem cell reprogramming in mouse ES/iPS cells and, as shown in this report, potentiates human DUX4 expression, suggests that DUX4 itself might facilitate reprogramming to the naive state and that mouse Dux and human DUX4 might be subject to similar regulation, a finding not entirely obvious given that these retrogenes are thought to have been generated by independent retrotranspositions of the parental DUXC gene, as noted above.
evidence: This is inferred from the data and prior work.
